notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg1701.tlg001.1st1K-gr: Chapter XII opens in the first person (‘while he was still saying these things to me’, ‘we too followed’), though Abraham is elsewhere in the third person; the Greek ἐμοὶ … λαλοῦντος is irregular. χαρζαναῖς, ‘whips’, is a rare word. Dokiel and Pyruel follow the text’s Δοκιήλ and Πυρουήλ.

κολακία, rendered ‘gentle coaxing’ and ‘gentleness’, is literally ‘flattery’. ὀλιγωρία θανάτου, ‘faintness of death’, uses ὀλιγωρία (normally ‘neglect’) for a swoon. In πρόσωπον ἀσπίδος ἀγριώτερον the genitive could instead be one of comparison: ‘a face more savage than an asp’.

nodes.text: XII. While he was still saying these things to me, behold, two angels, fiery in appearance, pitiless in mind and harsh in look; and they were driving myriads of souls, pitilessly beating them with fiery whips. And the angel was holding one soul. And they drove all the souls into the broad gate, toward destruction. So we too followed the angels and came inside that broad gate. And between the two gates stood a terrifying throne, in the appearance of terrifying crystal, flashing like fire. And upon it sat a wondrous man, bright as the sun, like a son of God. Before him stood a table like crystal, all of gold and fine linen. Upon the table lay a book, its thickness six cubits and its breadth ten cubits. To the right and left of it stood two angels holding papyrus and ink and pen. In front of the table sat a light-bearing angel, holding a balance in his hand; and on the left sat an angel all of fire, pitiless and harsh, holding in his hand a trumpet and holding within it all-devouring fire, the testing of sinners. And the wondrous man who sat upon the throne himself judged and sentenced the souls; and the two angels on the right and on the left recorded: the one on the right recorded the righteous deeds, and the one on the left the sins. And the one in front of the table, who held the balance, weighed the souls; and the fiery angel, who held the fire, tested the souls. And Abraham asked the commander-in-chief Michael: ‘What are these things that we are looking at?’ And the commander-in-chief said: ‘These things that you see, holy Abraham, are the judgment and the recompense.’ And behold, the angel who was holding the soul in his hand: he brought it before the judge. And the judge said to one of the angels who served him: ‘Open this book for me and find me the sins of this soul.’ And opening the book, he found its sins and its righteous deeds evenly balanced; and he handed it over neither to the tormentors nor to those being saved, but set it in the middle.

XIII. And Abraham said: ‘My lord commander-in-chief, who is this all-wondrous judge? And who are the angels who record? And who is the sun-like angel who holds the balance? And who is the fiery angel who holds the fire?’ And the commander-in-chief said: ‘Do you see, all-holy Abraham, the terrifying man seated upon the throne? This is the son of Adam the first-formed, who is called Abel, whom Cain the wicked killed. And he sits here to judge all creation, examining the righteous and the sinners. For God said: “I do not judge you, but every man shall be judged by a man.” For this reason he has given him judgment, to judge the world until his great and glorious coming. And then, righteous Abraham, comes the perfect judgment and recompense, eternal and unchangeable, which no one can review. For every man has been born of the first-formed, and for this reason they are first judged here by his son. And at the second coming they will be judged by the twelve tribes of Israel, every breath and every creature. And the third time they will be judged by the Master, God of all; and then at last the end of that judgment is near, and the sentence is terrifying, and there is no one to undo it. And so the judgment of the world and the recompense take place through three tribunals; and for this reason a matter is not finally established on one or two witnesses, but on three witnesses every word shall stand. The two angels, the one on the right and the one on the left, these are the ones who record the sins and the righteous deeds: the one on the right records the righteous deeds, and the one on the left the sins. The sun-like angel, who holds the balance in his hand, this is Dokiel the archangel, the just weigher, and he weighs the righteous deeds and the sins in the righteousness of God. And the fiery and pitiless angel, who holds the fire in his hand, this is Pyruel the archangel, who has authority over fire, and he tests the works of men by fire. And if the fire burns up anyone’s work, at once the angel of judgment takes him and carries him off to the place of sinners, a most bitter place of punishment. But if the fire tests anyone’s work and does not touch it, that man is justified, and the angel of righteousness takes him and carries him up to be saved in the lot of the righteous. And so, most righteous Abraham, all things in all are tested by fire and balance.’

XVI. Then the Most High says: ‘Call Death here to me, the one called the shameless face and the pitiless look.’ And Michael the incorporeal went off and said to Death: ‘Come; the Master of creation, the immortal King, calls you.’ When Death heard, he shuddered and trembled, gripped by great dread, and coming with great fear he stood before the invisible Father, shuddering, groaning and trembling, awaiting the Master’s command. So the invisible God says to Death: ‘Come, bitter and savage name of the world: hide your savagery, cover your rottenness, cast your bitterness away from you, and clothe yourself in your beauty and all your glory, and go down to my friend Abraham and take him and bring him to me. But I tell you this too, now: do not terrify him, but take him with gentle coaxing, for he is my true friend.’ When Death heard these things, he went out from the presence of the Most High and put on a most brilliant robe, and made his appearance sun-like, and became comely and beautiful beyond the sons of men, wearing the form of an archangel, his cheeks flashing with fire; and he went off to Abraham. Now righteous Abraham had gone out of his chamber and was sitting under the trees of Mamre, holding his chin in his hand and awaiting the coming of the archangel Michael. And behold, a scent of sweet fragrance came toward him, and a radiance of light; and turning round, Abraham saw Death coming toward him in great glory and beauty. And Abraham rose and went to meet him, thinking him to be the commander-in-chief of God. And Death, seeing him, bowed down before him, saying: ‘Hail, honoured Abraham, righteous soul, true friend of God Most High, and tent-companion of the holy angels.’ And Abraham said to Death: ‘Hail, you of sun-bright look, sun-formed, most glorious helper, light-bearer, wondrous man: from where does Your Glory come to us, and who are you, and from where have you come?’ So Death says: ‘Most righteous Abraham, see, I tell you the truth: I am the bitter cup of death.’ Abraham says to him: ‘No, rather you are the comeliness of the world, you are the glory and the beauty of angels and of men, you are fairer in form than every form; and you say, “I am the bitter cup of death,” and do not rather say, “I am fairer than every good thing”?’ And Death said: ‘I am telling you the truth: what God named me, that is what I tell you.’ And Abraham said: ‘For what have you come here?’ And Death said: ‘I have come for your holy soul.’ So Abraham says: ‘I know what you mean, but I will not follow you.’ And Death fell silent and did not answer him a word.

XVII. And Abraham rose and went into his house, and Death too followed him there. Abraham went up into his chamber, and Death too went up with him. Abraham lay down on his couch, and Death too came and sat by his feet. And Abraham said: ‘Go away, go away from me, for I wish to rest on my couch.’ Death says: ‘I will not withdraw until I take your spirit from you.’ Abraham says to him: ‘By the immortal God I charge you to tell me the truth: are you Death?’ Death says to him: ‘I am Death; I am the one who ravages the world.’ And Abraham said: ‘I beg you, since you are Death, tell me: do you go to everyone in this way, in such fairness of form and glory and beauty?’ And Death said: ‘No, my lord Abraham; for your righteous deeds, and the boundless sea of your hospitality, and the greatness of your love for God have become a crown upon my head; and in beauty and in great calm and gentleness I approach the righteous, but I approach sinners in great rottenness and savagery and the greatest bitterness, and with a savage and pitiless look.’ And Abraham said: ‘I beg you, listen to me and show me your savagery and all your rottenness and bitterness.’ And Death said: ‘You will not be able to behold my savagery, most righteous Abraham.’ And Abraham said: ‘Yes, I shall be able to behold all your savagery, for the sake of the name of the living God, because the power of my heavenly God is with me.’ Then Death stripped off all his beauty and comeliness, and all the glory and the sun-like form that he had worn, and put on a tyrant’s robe, and made his appearance gloomy, more savage than every kind of wild beast and more unclean than every uncleanness. And he showed Abraham seven fiery heads of dragons, and fourteen faces, of most flaming fire and great savagery: a dark face, and the most gloomy face of a viper, and the face of a most dreadful precipice, and the face of an asp, more savage still, and the face of a fearsome lion, and the face of a horned viper and of a basilisk. He showed also the face of a fiery broadsword, and a sword-bearing face, and the face of lightning flashing fearsomely, and the roar of fearsome thunder. He showed also another face, of a savage sea surging with waves, and a savage river seething, and a fearsome three-headed dragon, and a cup brimming with poisons; and, in a word, he showed him great savagery and unbearable bitterness and every deadly disease, as of the smell of death. And from the great bitterness and savagery menservants and maidservants died, about seven thousand in number; and righteous Abraham came into a faintness of death, so that his spirit failed.
